title: Work drying up in Chicago and the foundry job
summary: Music slowed in the mid-forties; he took laundry and foundry work with little playing.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Then I gather, well, like up in Chicago, you know, things started drying up a lot. I mean, it started.

Yeah, things started drying up around about, let's see, around, around, about, in the mid-forties, 45 or 46. Mm-hmm. I stopped playing with the most guys to stop, and I had a second wife there. And I went, I got a job in the lawn, just sorting out clothes, and I got to be what they call a spotter. That's slower Don than a friend of mine used to preach to you. He had a beautiful voice. And, can't think his name right now, he was working at a founder where he made the foam plows, you know. And I was scared when I went in that place there, but I knew I had two friends in the foamer, the black foamer and the white foamer on my side, so they made a barrel grind out of me. That's what foam, this is to put on the foam plow, and you have to soften them on the end, you know. It was hard work, but I stayed there until they started laying off.
But you were playing a little bit of music on his side?

A little bit of them, no, not too much music then. When I worked at that, I didn't play all that, I worked at that founder, I didn't play all the time playing completely. Because there were things that I was actually slowing down, you know, around 46, 47.
